what_its_for: Glatiramer is used to treat relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS). It helps reduce the number of MS flare-ups (relapses) you have. It does not cure MS, but it can help slow down how often your symptoms get worse.
how_to_take: Glatiramer is given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous injection). You will be trained by your healthcare provider or nurse on how to give yourself the injection at home. Rotate your injection sites each time — you can use your thighs, stomach (abdomen), upper arms, or hips. Never inject into the same spot twice in a row. Let the prefilled syringe warm up to room temperature for about 20 minutes before injecting. Do not shake the syringe.
dosing: There are two dosing options your doctor may prescribe: (1) 20 mg injected under the skin ONCE EVERY DAY, or (2) 40 mg injected under the skin THREE TIMES A WEEK (at least 48 hours apart, for example Monday, Wednesday, and Friday). Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not switch between dose options without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not almost time for your next scheduled dose. Never take two doses at the same time or on the same day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store glatiramer in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze it. Keep it away from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to one month, but do not put it back in the refrigerator after it has been at room temperature. Keep out of reach of children. Throw away used syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container — do not throw them in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid injecting into red, irritated, bruised, or tender skin. Avoid injecting into the same spot repeatedly, as this can cause lumps or skin changes under the skin. Do not use a syringe that looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it. Avoid getting pregnant while on glatiramer without talking to your doctor first, as it is not fully studied in pregnancy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: chest pain, heart pounding or racing, flushing (redness), shortness of breath, or anxiety immediately after your injection (this is called a post-injection reaction and usually passes within 15–30 minutes, but tell your doctor). Also contact your doctor if you notice: severe skin reactions, open sores, or hard lumps at injection sites; signs of infection (fever, chills, pain); signs of liver problems (yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine); swelling of your face, lips, or throat; or any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Glatiramer does not work overnight. Most patients do not notice immediate changes in how they feel. It works quietly in the background to reduce MS relapses over time. It may take several months or even up to 2 years before you and your doctor can see the full benefit. It is very important to keep taking it even if you feel fine — stopping it may allow your MS to become more active.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using glatiramer if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known if it is safe during pregnancy. Elderly patients: Glatiramer has not been widely studied in people over 65, so use with caution and follow your doctor's guidance. Children: Glatiramer is not approved for use in children under 18 years old. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems before starting this medication.
